text:
Of my grandfather Verus I have learned to be gentle and meek, and to
 refrain from all anger and passion. From the fame and memory of him that
 begot me I have learned both shamefastness and manlike behaviour. Of my
 mother I have learned to be religious, and bountiful; and to forbear, not
 only to do, but to intend any evil; to content myself with a spare diet,
 and to fly all such excess as is incidental to great wealth.
plain_text: From my grandfather Verus I learned to be gentle and calm, and to hold back anger. From the memory of my father I learned both humility and strength of character. From my mother I learned devotion and generosity. She taught me not only to avoid doing wrong, but to avoid even wanting to do wrong. From her I also learned to be content with simple food and to stay away from the excess that wealth can bring.

text:
Of my
 great-grandfather, both to frequent public schools and auditories, and to
 get me good and able teachers at home; and that I ought not to think much,
 if upon such occasions, I were at excessive charges.
plain_text: From my great-grandfather I learned to value good schools and good teachers, and not to worry about the cost of a proper education.

text:
Of him that brought me up, not to be fondly addicted to either of
 the two great factions of the coursers in the circus, called Prasini, and
 Veneti: nor in the amphitheatre partially to favour any of the gladiators,
 or fencers, as either the Parmularii, or the Secutores. Moreover, to
 endure labour; nor to need many things; when I have anything to do, to do
 it myself rather than by others; not to meddle with many businesses; and
 not easily to admit of any slander.
plain_text: From my tutor I learned not to get caught up in the rival teams at the races, whether the Greens or the Blues. I learned not to take sides among the gladiators or fighters at the arena. I learned to work hard, to need little, to do things myself rather than through others, not to take on too many concerns, and not to listen to gossip.

text:
Of Diognetus, not to busy myself about vain things, and not easily
 to believe those things, which are commonly spoken, by such as take upon
 them to work wonders, and by sorcerers, or prestidigitators, and
 impostors; concerning the power of charms, and their driving out of
 demons, or evil spirits; and the like. Not to keep quails for the game;
 nor to be mad after such things. Not to be offended with other men's
 liberty of speech, and to apply myself unto philosophy.
plain_text: From Diognetus I learned not to waste time on pointless things. I learned not to believe those who claim to work wonders — sorcerers, magicians, and frauds — or their talk of charms and casting out spirits and such. I learned not to keep birds for sport or get carried away by such pastimes. I learned not to be bothered when others speak freely, and to give myself to philosophy.

text:
Him also I must
 thank, that ever I heard first Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus, and
 that I did write dialogues in my youth; and that I took liking to the
 philosophers' little couch and skins, and such other things, which by the
 Grecian discipline are proper to those who profess philosophy.
plain_text: I must also thank him that I first heard Bacchius, then Tandasis and Marcianus, and that I wrote dialogues when I was young. I also came to appreciate the simple bed and animal skins and other plain things that belong to the Greek way of studying philosophy.

text:
To Rusticus I am beholding, that I first entered into the conceit
 that my life wanted some redress and cure. And then, that I did not fall
 into the ambition of ordinary sophists, either to write tracts concerning
 the common theorems, or to exhort men unto virtue and the study of
 philosophy by public orations; as also that I never by way of ostentation
 did affect to show myself an active able man, for any kind of bodily
 exercises. And that I gave over the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of
 elegant neat language.
plain_text: To Rusticus I owe the realization that my character needed work and improvement. From him I learned not to fall into the habits of common intellectuals — writing essays on abstract ideas, or giving grand speeches urging people toward virtue. I learned not to show off my physical ability or make a display of myself. I gave up the study of fine speaking, poetry, and elegant language.

That I did not use to walk about the house in my
 long robe, nor to do any such things. Moreover I learned of him to write
 letters without any affectation, or curiosity; such as that was, which by
 him was written to my mother from Sinuessa: and to be easy and ready to be

plain_text: I learned not to walk around the house in fancy robes, or do anything like that for show. From him I also learned to write letters in a simple, honest way — like the one he wrote to my mother from Sinuessa. And I learned to be quick to forgive and make peace with anyone who had upset me, as soon as they were willing to come back.

To read with

plain_text: I learned to read carefully, not to settle for a shallow understanding, and not to quickly agree with popular opinions. I must also thank him for introducing me to the writings of Epictetus — his moral notes and reflections — which Rusticus gave to me from his own collection.

text:
From Apollonius, true liberty, and unvariable steadfastness, and not
 to regard anything at all, though never so little, but right and reason: and always, whether in the sharpest pains, or after the loss of a child, or in long diseases, to be still the same man; who also was a present and
 visible example unto me, that it was possible for the same man to be both
 vehement and remiss: a man not subject to be vexed, and offended with the
 incapacity of his scholars and auditors in his lectures and expositions; and a true pattern of a man who of all his good gifts and faculties,
plain_text: From Apollonius I learned true freedom and steady resolve — to pay attention to nothing, however small, except what is right and reasonable. I learned to remain the same person whether in sharp pain, after the loss of a child, or during long illness. He showed me by his own example that the same person can be both intense and relaxed. He was a man who never grew angry at students who struggled to understand his lessons. He was a true example of someone who, among all his fine qualities,

least
 esteemed in himself, that his excellent skill and ability to teach and

plain_text: considered least impressive his own excellent skill in teaching and explaining the core ideas of Stoic philosophy.

text:
Of
 him also I learned how to receive favours and kindnesses (as commonly they
 are accounted:) from friends, so that I might not become obnoxious unto
 them, for them, nor more yielding upon occasion, than in right I ought;
 and yet so that I should not pass them neither, as an unsensible and

plain_text: From him I also learned how to accept favors and kindness from friends without becoming dependent on them or feeling overly obligated — and yet without ignoring their generosity or seeming ungrateful.

text:
Of Sextus, mildness and the pattern of a family governed with
 paternal affection; and a purpose to live according to nature: to be grave
 without affectation: to observe carefully the several dispositions of my
 friends, not to be offended with idiots, nor unseasonably to set upon
 those that are carried with the vulgar opinions, with the theorems, and
 tenets of philosophers: his conversation being an example how a man might
 accommodate himself to all men and companies; so that though his company
 were sweeter and more pleasing than any flatterer's cogging and fawning;
plain_text: From Sextus I learned gentleness, and the example of a household led with fatherly love. I learned to live according to nature, and to be serious without pretending. I learned to pay close attention to the character of my friends, not to look down on simple people, and not to lecture those who follow popular opinions with philosophical arguments at the wrong time. His way of talking showed how a person could fit in with anyone and any group. His company was more pleasant than any flatterer's praise,

yet was it at the same time most respected and reverenced: who also had a
 proper happiness and faculty, rationally and methodically to find out, and
 set in order all necessary determinations and instructions for a man's

plain_text: yet at the same time he was deeply respected. He also had a gift for discovering and organizing, in a clear and orderly way, all the principles a person needs for living well.

text:
A man without ever the least appearance of anger, or any other
 passion; able at the same time most exactly to observe the Stoic 
Apathia
,
 or unpassionateness, and yet to be most tender-hearted: ever of good
 credit; and yet almost without any noise, or rumour: very learned, and yet
 making little show.
plain_text: He was a man who never showed the least trace of anger or any strong emotion. He practiced the Stoic calm perfectly, and yet he was deeply compassionate. He had a fine reputation, but without drawing attention to himself. He was very learned, yet made no show of it.

text:
From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not
 reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or any
 false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony, or
 confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to utter it
 as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect
 admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.
plain_text: From Alexander the Grammarian I learned not to criticize others harshly for mistakes in speech — for a wrong word, a clumsy phrase, or a mispronunciation. Instead, I learned to gently use the correct form myself in my reply, as if I had not noticed the error, or to find some other tactful and polite way to let the person know.

text:
Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a
 tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called
 εὐπατρίδαι,
 
i.e.
 nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void of natural
 affection.
plain_text: From Fronto I learned how much envy, dishonesty, and pretense surround the life of a tyrant, and how those who are called nobly born are in some ways lacking in genuine warmth and feeling.

text:
Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to
 say, or to write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure'; nor in
 this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends and
 acquaintances (to every one in his kind) under pretence of urgent affairs.
plain_text: From Alexander the Platonist I learned not to say or write to anyone, unless truly necessary, "I am too busy." I learned not to keep putting off the duties I owe to friends and those I know, using the excuse of pressing business.

text:
Of Catulus, not to contemn any friend's expostulation, though unjust,
 but to strive to reduce him to his former disposition: freely and heartily
 to speak well of all my masters upon any occasion, as it is reported of
 Domitius, and Athenodotus: and to love my children with true affection.
plain_text: From Catulus I learned not to dismiss a friend's complaint, even if it seems unfair, but to try to restore the friendship to what it was before. I learned to speak well of all my teachers sincerely and gladly, as Domitius and Athenodotus were said to do. And I learned to love my children with real affection.

text:
From my brother Severus, to be kind and loving to all them of my
 house and family; by whom also I came to the knowledge of Thrasea and
 Helvidius, and Cato, and Dio, and Brutus. He it was also that did put me
 in the first conceit and desire of an equal commonwealth, administered by
 justice and equality; and of a kingdom wherein should be regarded nothing
 more than the good and welfare of the subjects.
plain_text: From my brother Severus I learned to be kind and loving to everyone in my household and family. Through him I came to know of Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus. He was the one who first gave me the idea of a fair government, run with justice and equality — a state where nothing matters more than the good and well-being of its people.

text:
Of him also, to observe a
 constant tenor, (not interrupted, with any other cares and distractions,)
 in the study and esteem of philosophy: to be bountiful and liberal in the
 largest measure; always to hope the best; and to be confident that my
 friends love me. In whom I moreover observed open dealing towards those
 whom he reproved at any time, and that his friends might without all doubt
 or much observation know what he would, or would not, so open and plain
 was he.
plain_text: From him I also learned to hold steady in my devotion to philosophy, without letting other worries and distractions pull me away. I learned to be generous in the fullest sense, to always hope for the best, and to trust that my friends truly care for me. I also saw in him an honest directness toward those he corrected, and his friends could always tell, without guessing, what he wanted or did not want — so open and straightforward was he.

text:
From Claudius Maximus, in all things to endeavour to have power
 of myself, and in nothing to be carried about; to be cheerful and
 courageous in all sudden chances and accidents, as in sicknesses: to love
 mildness, and moderation, and gravity: and to do my business, whatsoever
 it be, thoroughly, and without querulousness. Whatsoever he said, all men
 believed him that as he spake, so he thought, and whatsoever he did, that
 he did it with a good intent.
plain_text: From Claudius Maximus I learned to have control over myself in all things, and not to be pushed around by circumstances. I learned to be cheerful and brave in the face of sudden troubles and illness, and to value gentleness, moderation, and seriousness. I learned to do whatever work I had to do thoroughly and without complaining. Everyone believed that he meant what he said, and that whatever he did, he did with good intentions.

text:
His manner was, never to wonder at anything;
 never to be in haste, and yet never slow: nor to be perplexed, or
 dejected, or at any time unseemly, or excessively to laugh: nor to be
 angry, or suspicious, but ever ready to do good, and to forgive, and to
 speak truth; and all this, as one that seemed rather of himself to have
 been straight and right, than ever to have been rectified or redressed;
 neither was there any man that ever thought himself undervalued by him, or
 that could find in his heart, to think himself a better man than he. He
 would also be very pleasant and gracious.
plain_text: His way was never to be surprised by anything, never to rush, and yet never to be slow. He was never confused or downcast, never awkward or given to laughing too much. He was never angry or suspicious, but always ready to do good, to forgive, and to speak the truth. All of this came naturally to him, as if he had always been upright, rather than having been corrected along the way. No one ever felt looked down upon by him, and no one could honestly believe himself to be a better person. He was also warm and gracious.

text:
In my father, I observed his meekness; his constancy without
 wavering in those things, which after a due examination and deliberation,
 he had determined.
plain_text: In my father, I saw his gentleness — and his firmness, without wavering, in the decisions he had carefully thought through.

text:
How free from all vanity he carried himself in matter
 of honour and dignity, (as they are esteemed:) his laboriousness and
 assiduity, his readiness to hear any man, that had aught to say tending to
 any common good: how generally and impartially he would give every man his
 due; his skill and knowledge, when rigour or extremity, or when remissness
 or moderation was in season; how he did abstain from all unchaste love of
 youths; his moderate condescending to other men's occasions as an ordinary
 man, neither absolutely requiring of his friends,
plain_text: How free he was from vanity when it came to honors and titles. How hardworking and tireless he was. How willing to listen to anyone who had something to say for the common good. How fairly and impartially he gave each person their due. His sense for when to be strict and when to be lenient. How he stayed away from improper desires. How he went along with others' needs as any ordinary person would, without demanding that his friends

text:
His accurate examination of things in consultations, and
 patient hearing of others. He would not hastily give over the search of
 the matter, as one easy to be satisfied with sudden notions and
 apprehensions. His care to preserve his friends; how neither at any time
 he would carry himself towards them with disdainful neglect, and grow
 weary of them; nor yet at any time be madly fond of them. His contented
 mind in all things, his cheerful countenance, his care to foresee things
 afar off, and to take order for the least, without any noise or clamour.
plain_text: His careful way of examining matters in meetings, and his patience in hearing others. He would not cut short an investigation, as someone too easily satisfied with quick impressions might do. His care to keep his friends close — never treating them with cold neglect or growing tired of them, and never becoming foolishly attached to them either. His contented spirit in all things, his cheerful face, his habit of looking ahead and planning for even the smallest details, all without fuss or commotion.

text:
Moreover how all acclamations and flattery were repressed by him: how
 carefully he observed all things necessary to the government, and kept an
 account of the common expenses, and how patiently he did abide that he was
 reprehended by some for this his strict and rigid kind of dealing.
plain_text: How he put a stop to all cheering and flattery directed at him. How carefully he attended to everything the government required, and kept track of public spending. And how patiently he bore the criticism from those who called his management too strict and rigid.

text:
How he
 was neither a superstitious worshipper of the gods, nor an ambitious
 pleaser of men, or studious of popular applause; but sober in all things,
 and everywhere observant of that which was fitting; no affecter of
 novelties: in those things which conduced to his ease and convenience,
 (plenty whereof his fortune did afford him,) without pride and bragging,
 yet with all freedom and liberty: so that as he did freely enjoy them
 without any anxiety or affectation when they were present; so when absent,
 he found no want of them.
plain_text: He was not superstitious in his worship, nor eager to please people or chase popular approval. He was measured in all things and always mindful of what was proper. He did not chase after new things for their own sake. As for the comforts his good fortune provided — and there were many — he enjoyed them freely, without pride or show, and without anxiety. But when they were absent, he did not miss them either.

text:
Moreover, that he was never commended by any
 man, as either a learned acute man, or an obsequious officious man, or a
 fine orator; but as a ripe mature man, a perfect sound man; one that could
 not endure to be flattered; able to govern both himself and others.
plain_text: No one praised him as a clever scholar, an overly helpful busybody, or a fine speaker. Instead, they praised him as a mature and complete person — one who could not stand flattery, and who was able to govern both himself and others.

text:

 those that were not so; his sociableness, his gracious and delightful
 conversation, but never unto satiety; his care of his body within bounds

 neatness, and elegancy; and yet not as one that did not regard it: so that

 any that had obtained any peculiar faculty, as either eloquence,
plain_text: How greatly he honored all true philosophers, without looking down on those who were not. His warm and enjoyable conversation, which never went on too long. His care for his body — kept within proper limits, not because he wanted to live as long as possible or was overly concerned with appearance, but not neglecting it either. Because of this balanced care, he rarely needed medicine or treatment. And especially how willingly he gave way to anyone who had a particular talent, such as eloquence,

And although he carefully followed the old customs of his ancestors, he did not want people to notice or think he was deliberately imitating the old ways.

text:
Again, how he was not easily
 moved and tossed up and down, but loved to be constant, both in the same
 places and businesses; and how after his great fits of headache he would
 return fresh and vigorous to his wonted affairs. Again, that secrets he

 his discretion and moderation, in exhibiting of the public sights and

plain_text: He was not easily unsettled or thrown off course, but preferred to stay steady in the same places and the same work. After severe headaches, he would return fresh and strong to his usual duties. He kept few secrets, and those only about public affairs. His good judgment and moderation showed in the public games and shows he put on for the people, in public buildings, in gifts to the citizens, and in all such things.

text:
In all these things, having a respect unto men
 only as men, and to the equity of the things themselves, and not unto the
 glory that might follow. Never wont to use the baths at unseasonable
 hours; no builder; never curious, or solicitous, either about his meat, or
 about the workmanship, or colour of his clothes, or about anything that
 belonged to external beauty.
plain_text: In all these things, he cared about people as people and about the fairness of the matter itself, not about the glory that might follow. He did not use the baths at odd hours. He was not a builder of grand projects. He was never fussy about his food, or the style or color of his clothes, or anything to do with outward appearance.

text:
In all his conversation, far from all
 inhumanity, all boldness, and incivility, all greediness and impetuosity;
 never doing anything with such earnestness, and intention, that a man
 could say of him, that he did sweat about it: but contrariwise, all things
 distinctly, as at leisure; without trouble; orderly, soundly, and
 agreeably.
plain_text: In all his dealings, he was far from any cruelty, rudeness, or greed. He never rushed into anything with such intensity that you could say he was straining over it. On the contrary, he did everything calmly, as if he had all the time in the world — without stress, in good order, steadily, and pleasantly.

text:
A man might have applied that to him, which is recorded of
 Socrates, that he knew how to want, and to enjoy those things, in the want
 whereof, most men show themselves weak; and in the fruition, intemperate:
 but to hold out firm and constant, and to keep within the compass of true
 moderation and sobriety in either estate, is proper to a man, who hath a
 perfect and invincible soul; such as he showed himself in the sickness of
 Maximus.
plain_text: You could say of him what was said of Socrates — that he knew how to go without things, and how to enjoy them too. Most people are weak when they lack things, and excessive when they have them. But to remain firm and balanced, keeping to true moderation whether in plenty or in want — that belongs to a person with a strong and unshakeable soul. He showed himself to be such a person during the illness of Maximus.

text:
From the gods I received that I had good grandfathers, and parents,
 a good sister, good masters, good domestics, loving kinsmen, almost all
 that I have; and that I never through haste and rashness transgressed
 against any of them, notwithstanding that my disposition was such, as that
 such a thing (if occasion had been) might very well have been committed by
 me, but that It was the mercy of the gods, to prevent such a concurring of
 matters and occasions, as might make me to incur this blame.
plain_text: From the gods I received good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good servants, and loving relatives — nearly everything I have. And I never, through haste or carelessness, wronged any of them. My nature was such that I could have done so if the circumstances had come together. But it was the mercy of the gods that no such combination of events arose to lead me into that fault.

text:
That I was
 not long brought up by the concubine of my father; that I preserved the
 flower of my youth. That I took not upon me to be a man before my time,
 but rather put it off longer than I needed.
plain_text: That I was not raised for long by my father's mistress. That I kept my innocence in youth. That I did not try to act grown up before my time, and even waited longer than I needed to.

text:
That I lived under the
 government of my lord and father, who would take away from me all pride
 and vainglory, and reduce me to that conceit and opinion that it was not
 impossible for a prince to live in the court without a troop of guards and
 followers, extraordinary apparel, such and such torches and statues, and
 other like particulars of state and magnificence; but that a man may
 reduce and contract himself almost to the state of a private man, and yet
 for all that not to become the more base and remiss in those public
 matters and affairs, wherein power and authority is requisite.
plain_text: That I was raised under my father's guidance, who stripped away all my pride and showed me that a ruler can live at court without a crowd of guards and servants, without fancy clothes, special torches, statues, or any other trappings of royal display. He showed me that a person can live almost like an ordinary citizen and still carry out public duties with full strength and authority when it is called for.

text:
That I have
 had such a brother, who by his own example might stir me up to think of
 myself; and by his respect and love, delight and please me. That I have
 got ingenuous children, and that they were not born distorted, nor with
 any other natural deformity. That I was no great proficient in the study
 of rhetoric and poetry, and of other faculties, which perchance I might
 have dwelt upon, if I had found myself to go on in them with success.
plain_text: That I had a brother whose example inspired me to look at myself, and whose respect and love brought me happiness. That my children were born healthy and without any disability. That I did not become too skilled in rhetoric, poetry, or other such studies — subjects I might have lingered on if I had found I was good at them.

text:
That
 I did by times prefer those, by whom I was brought up, to such places and
 dignities, which they seemed unto me most to desire; and that I did not
 put them off with hope and expectation, that (since that they were yet but
 young) I would do the same hereafter. That I ever knew Apollonius and
 Rusticus, and Maximus.
plain_text: That I promoted those who raised me to the positions and honors they most desired, without delay — not putting them off with promises that I would do so later, since they were still young. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus.

text:
That I have had occasion often and effectually to
 consider and meditate with myself, concerning that life which is according
 to nature, what the nature and manner of it is: so that as for the gods
 and such suggestions, helps and inspirations, as might be expected from
 them, nothing did hinder, but that I might have begun long before to live
 according to nature; or that even now that I was not yet partaker and in
 present possession of that life, that I myself (in that I did not observe
 those inward motions, and suggestions,
plain_text: That I have had many chances to think deeply about what it means to live according to nature — what such a life truly looks like. As far as the gods are concerned, and whatever help and guidance they offered, nothing stopped me from living this way long ago. And if I still have not fully reached that life, the fault is my own — because I did not follow those inner promptings and

yea and almost plain and apparent
 instructions and admonitions of the gods,) was the only cause of it.
plain_text: what were nearly clear and obvious instructions from the gods — I alone am the cause of that failure.

text:
That
 my body in such a life, hath been able to hold out so long. That I never
 had to do with Benedicta and Theodotus, yea and afterwards when I fell
 into some fits of love, I was soon cured. That having been often
 displeased with Rusticus, I never did him anything for which afterwards I
 had occasion to repent. That it being so that my mother was to die young,
