plain_text: That my body has held up so long through such a life. That I never became involved with Benedicta or Theodotus, and that even later, when I fell into bouts of desire, I recovered quickly. That although I was often frustrated with Rusticus, I never did anything to him that I later had reason to regret. That although my mother was destined to die young, she still spent her final years with me.

text:
That as often as I had a
 purpose to help and succour any that either were poor, or fallen into some
 present necessity, I never was answered by my officers that there was not
 ready money enough to do it; and that I myself never had occasion to
 require the like succour from any other. That I have such a wife, so
 obedient, so loving, so ingenuous. That I had choice of fit and able men,
 to whom I might commit the bringing up of my children.
plain_text: That whenever I wanted to help someone who was poor or in need, my officials never told me there was not enough money. And that I myself never had to ask for such help from anyone else. That I have a wife so loyal, so loving, so honest. That I was able to find good and capable people to raise my children.

text:
That by dreams I
 have received help, as for other things, so in particular, how I might
 stay my casting of blood, and cure my dizziness, as that also that
 happened to thee in Cajeta, as unto Chryses when he prayed by the
 seashore. And when I did first apply myself to philosophy, that I did not
 fall into the hands of some sophists, or spent my time either in reading
 the manifold volumes of ordinary philosophers, nor in practising myself in
 the solution of arguments and fallacies, nor dwelt upon the studies of the
 meteors, and other natural curiosities.
plain_text: That through dreams I received help — especially for stopping my coughing up blood and curing my dizzy spells, as happened at Cajeta, like Chryses praying by the seashore. And that when I first turned to philosophy, I did not fall in with clever talkers, or waste my time reading stacks of ordinary philosophy books, or practicing how to solve tricky arguments and riddles, or dwell on the study of weather patterns and other natural curiosities.

text:
All these things without the
 assistance of the gods, and fortune, could not have been.
plain_text: None of these things could have happened without the help of the gods and of fortune.

text:
In the country of the Quadi at Granua, these. Betimes in the morning
 say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with
 an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an
 unsociable uncharitable man. All these ill qualities have happened unto
 them, through ignorance of that which is truly good and truly bad.
plain_text: Written among the Quadi, at the Granua river. Say to yourself first thing in the morning: today I will meet someone meddling and ungrateful, someone rude, someone deceitful or jealous, someone cold and selfish. All of these faults have come upon them because they do not know what is truly good and what is truly bad.

text:
But I
 that understand the nature of that which is good, that it only is to be
 desired, and of that which is bad, that it only is truly odious and
 shameful: who know moreover, that this transgressor, whosoever he be, is
 my kinsman, not by the same blood and seed, but by participation of the
 same reason, and of the same divine particle; How can I either be hurt by
 any of those, since it is not in their power to make me incur anything
 that is truly reproachful? or angry, and ill affected towards him, who by
 nature is so near unto me?
plain_text: But I understand what is truly good — that only virtue deserves to be desired — and what is truly bad — that only vice is shameful. And I know that whoever wrongs me is my relative, not through blood, but because we share the same reason and the same spark of the divine. How then can any of them truly hurt me, since they have no power to make me do anything disgraceful? And how can I be angry at someone who is, by nature, so close to me?

text:
for we are all born to be fellow-workers, as
 the feet, the hands, and the eyelids; as the rows of the upper and under
 teeth: for such therefore to be in opposition, is against nature; and what
 is it to chafe at, and to be averse from, but to be in opposition?
plain_text: For we are all born to work together, like the feet, the hands, and the eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To work against each other is against nature. And to resent someone or turn away from them is to work against them.

text:
Whatsoever I am, is either flesh, or life, or that which we
 commonly call the mistress and overruling part of man; reason. Away with
 thy books, suffer not thy mind any more to be distracted, and carried to
 and fro; for it will not be; but as even now ready to die, think little of
 thy flesh: blood, bones, and a skin; a pretty piece of knit and twisted
 work, consisting of nerves, veins and arteries; think no more of it, than
 so. And as for thy life, consider what it is; a wind; not one constant
 wind neither, but every moment of an hour let out, and sucked in again.
plain_text: Whatever I am is either flesh, or life, or what we call the ruling part of a person — reason. Put your books aside. Do not let your mind be scattered and pulled in every direction any longer, for you do not have time. Since you may die at any moment, think little of your flesh: it is blood, bones, and skin — a woven web of nerves, veins, and arteries, nothing more. As for your life, consider what it is: a breath. Not even a steady one, but one that is breathed out and drawn in again, moment by moment.

text:
The third, is thy ruling part; and here consider; Thou art an old man;
 suffer not that excellent part to be brought in subjection, and to become
 slavish: suffer it not to be drawn up and down with unreasonable and
 unsociable lusts and motions, as it were with wires and nerves; suffer it
 not any more, either to repine at anything now present, or to fear and fly
 anything to come, which the destiny hath appointed thee.
plain_text: The third part is your ruling mind. Consider this: you are an old man. Do not let that highest part of you be enslaved. Do not let it be pulled around by irrational and selfish desires, as if by strings. Do not let it complain about the present, or fear and flee from whatever the future has in store for you.

text:
Whatsoever proceeds from the gods immediately, that any man will
 grant totally depends from their divine providence. As for those things
 that are commonly said to happen by fortune, even those must be conceived
 to have dependence from nature, or from that first and general connection,
 and concatenation of all those things, which more apparently by the divine
 providence are administered and brought to pass.
plain_text: Whatever comes directly from the gods, anyone will agree, depends entirely on divine providence. And even those things that are said to happen by chance must be understood as connected to nature, or to that great chain of causes and events, all of which are governed and brought about by divine providence.

text:
All things flow from
 thence: and whatsoever it is that is, is both necessary, and conducing to
 the whole (part of which thou art), and whatsoever it is that is requisite
 and necessary for the preservation of the general, must of necessity for
 every particular nature, be good and behoveful. And as for the whole, it
 is preserved, as by the perpetual mutation and conversion of the simple
 elements one into another, so also by the mutation, and alteration of
 things mixed and compounded. Let these things suffice thee; let them be
 always unto thee, as thy general rules and precepts.
plain_text: Everything flows from that source. Whatever exists is both necessary and useful to the whole — of which you are a part. And whatever is needed to preserve the whole must also, by necessity, be good for each individual nature within it. The whole is sustained both by the constant change of the basic elements into one another, and by the change and rearrangement of more complex things. Let this be enough for you. Let these be your constant principles and rules.

text:
As for thy thirst
 after books, away with it with all speed, that thou die not murmuring and
 complaining, but truly meek and well satisfied, and from thy heart
 thankful unto the gods. THE FOURTH BOOK
plain_text: As for your craving for books, let it go quickly, so that you do not die grumbling and complaining, but truly at peace and content, and grateful to the gods from the heart.

text:
That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural
 temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and
 affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be,
 and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at first
 it intended.
plain_text: The ruling part of the mind, when it is in its true natural state, is always ready to adjust. When what it originally planned cannot be done, it easily turns to what can be done — to what is within its own power.

text:
For it never doth absolutely addict and apply itself to any
 one object, but whatsoever it is that it doth now intend and prosecute, it
 doth prosecute it with exception and reservation; so that whatsoever it is
 that falls out contrary to its first intentions, even that afterwards it
 makes its proper object.
plain_text: For it never locks itself entirely onto one goal. Whatever it pursues, it pursues with flexibility and openness. So whatever happens contrary to its first plan, it takes that new situation and makes it the thing to work with.

text:
Even as the fire when it prevails upon those
 things that are in his way; by which things indeed a little fire would
 have been quenched, but a great fire doth soon turn to its own nature, and
 so consume whatsoever comes in his way: yea by those very things it is
 made greater and greater.
plain_text: It is like a fire that overcomes whatever falls in its path. A small fire would be put out by such obstacles, but a great fire quickly turns them into fuel and grows even stronger because of them.

text:
Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according
 to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
plain_text: Let nothing be done carelessly or at random. Do everything according to the best and most careful principles.

text:
They seek for themselves private retiring
 places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself
 art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know
 proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou
 wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and
 free from all businesses.
plain_text: People look for places to get away — country houses, the seashore, the mountains. You yourself have often wished for such escapes. But this is a sign of great ignorance. At any moment you wish, you have the power to retreat into yourself and find rest, free from all concerns.

text:
A man cannot any whither retire better than to
 his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things
 within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may
 presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I
 understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all
 confusion and tumultuousness. Afford then thyself this retiring
 continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself.
plain_text: There is no better place to retreat than into your own soul — especially when you have stored up within yourself the kind of thoughts that bring instant peace and calm the moment you turn inward. By peace I mean a well-ordered inner life, free from confusion and noise. Give yourself this retreat often, and let it refresh and renew you.

text:
Let these precepts be
 brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may
 suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well
 pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this
 short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For what
 is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when
 thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are
 made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend?
plain_text: Keep your guiding principles short and basic, so that the moment you recall them, they are enough to clear your mind and send you back at peace with whatever you must face. For what is it that upsets you? The wickedness of other people? Remember that all rational beings were made for one another. That bearing with others is part of justice. That people do wrong without meaning to.

text:
and how many already,
 who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and
 fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto
 ashes? It is time for thee to make an end. As for those things which among
 the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and
 portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call
 that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his
 atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is
 as it were one city?
plain_text: And remember how many people who once hated, suspected, and fought bitterly against each other are now long since turned to ashes. It is time to let go. As for the things that happen to you as part of life's ordinary course, can you really be upset by any of them when you recall the basic question: either there is a guiding providence, or there are only atoms — and either way, we showed that the whole world is like one city?

text:
And as for thy body, what canst thou fear, if thou
 dost consider that thy mind and understanding, when once it hath
 recollected itself, and knows its own power, hath in this life and breath
 (whether it run smoothly and gently, or whether harshly and rudely), no
 interest at all, but is altogether indifferent: and whatsoever else thou
 hast heard and assented unto concerning either pain or pleasure? But the
 care of thine honour and reputation will perchance distract thee?
plain_text: And what about your body — what is there to fear? Consider that your mind, once it has gathered itself and knows its own strength, has no real stake in this bodily life — whether it goes smoothly or roughly — and is altogether indifferent. Remember also what you have already accepted about pain and pleasure. But perhaps it is concern for your reputation that distracts you?

text:
How can
 that be, if thou dost look back, and consider both how quickly all things
 that are, are forgotten, and what an immense chaos of eternity was before,
 and will follow after all things: and the vanity of praise, and the
 inconstancy and variableness of human judgments and opinions, and the
 narrowness of the place, wherein it is limited and circumscribed? For the
 whole earth is but as one point; and of it, this inhabited part of it, is
 but a very little part; and of this part, how many in number, and what
 manner of men are they, that will commend thee?
plain_text: How can that be, when you look back and see how quickly everything is forgotten? Consider the vast emptiness of time that stretches before and after all things. Consider how hollow praise is, how changeable human opinions are, and how small the space is where your name can even be known. The whole earth is just a point, and the part of it where people live is only a tiny fraction. And of that fraction, how many people, and what kind of people, will actually praise you?

text:
What remains then, but
 that thou often put in practice this kind of retiring of thyself, to this
 little part of thyself; and above all things, keep thyself from
 distraction, and intend not anything vehemently, but be free and consider
 all things, as a man whose proper object is Virtue, as a man whose true
 nature is to be kind and sociable, as a citizen, as a mortal creature. Among other things, which to consider, and look into thou must use to
 withdraw thyself, let those two be among the most obvious and at hand.
plain_text: What is left, then, but to practice this retreat into yourself — into this small part of you — again and again? Above all, keep yourself free from distraction. Do not pursue anything with too much force. Instead, remain open and consider all things as a person whose purpose is virtue, whose nature is to be kind and connected to others, who is a citizen, who is mortal. Among the things you return to in this inner retreat, let these two be the most ready at hand.

text:
One, that the things or objects themselves reach not unto the soul, but
 stand without still and quiet, and that it is from the opinion only which
 is within, that all the tumult and all the trouble doth proceed. The next,
 that all these things, which now thou seest, shall within a very little
 while be changed, and be no more: and ever call to mind, how many changes
 and alterations in the world thou thyself hast already been an eyewitness
 of in thy time. This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
plain_text: First, that things themselves do not reach the soul. They stand outside, still and quiet. All the turmoil and trouble comes only from the opinions you hold within. Second, that everything you see now will very soon change and be gone. Keep in mind how many changes you yourself have already witnessed. The world is nothing but change, and life is nothing but how you see it.

text:
If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then
 is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all. If
 reason is general, then is that reason also, which prescribeth what is to
 be done and what not, common unto all. If that, then law. If law, then are
 we fellow-citizens. If so, then are we partners in some one commonweal. If
 so, then the world is as it were a city. For which other commonweal is it,
 that all men can be said to be members of? From this common city it is,
 that understanding, reason, and law is derived unto us, for from whence
 else?
plain_text: If the ability to think and be reasonable is shared by all people, then the reason that makes us rational is shared by all. If reason is shared, then so is the sense of what should and should not be done. If that is shared, then so is law. If we share law, then we are fellow citizens. If we are fellow citizens, then we belong to one shared community. If so, then the world itself is like a city. For what other community could all people be said to belong to? From this common city come our understanding, our reason, and our law — where else could they come from?

text:
For as that which in me is earthly I have from some common earth;
 and that which is moist from some other element is imparted; as my breath
 and life hath its proper fountain; and that likewise which is dry and
 fiery in me: (for there is nothing which doth not proceed from something;
 as also there is nothing that can be reduced unto mere nothing:) so also
 is there some common beginning from whence my understanding hath
 proceeded.
plain_text: For just as the earthy part of me comes from the common earth, and the moist part from another element, and my breath and life from their own source, and the dry and fiery part from yet another — since nothing comes from nothing, and nothing can be reduced to nothing — so too my understanding must come from some common source.

text:
As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a
 mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely
 which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and
 consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or
 incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man
 himself.
plain_text: Just as birth is a mystery of nature, so is death — a mixture of elements coming apart and returning to the same elements again. There is nothing shameful in it. It is one in a series of natural events that a rational being goes through, and it is neither improper nor at odds with what a human being truly is.

text:
Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity
 proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would
 have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this,
 that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and
 after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be
 remaining.
plain_text: Certain things must necessarily follow from certain causes. Wishing they would not happen is like wishing a fig tree could grow without sap or water. Remember this above all: in a very short time, both you and the other person will be dead, and not long after that, even your names and memories will be gone.

text:
Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
 If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such
 thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make
 his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly.
 It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.
plain_text: Take away the opinion, and no one will feel wronged. If no one feels wronged, then there is no wrong. What does not make a person worse cannot make their life worse, and it cannot hurt them, inside or out. Nature made it this way for good reason, and so it is necessary.

text:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if
 thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it. I say not only in right
 order by a series of inevitable consequences, but according to justice and
 as it were by way of equal distribution, according to the true worth of
 everything. Continue then to take notice of it, as thou hast begun, and
 whatsoever thou dost, do it not without this proviso, that it be a thing
 of that nature that a good man (as the word good is properly taken) may do
 it. This observe carefully in every action.
plain_text: Whatever happens in the world happens justly. Pay close attention and you will see it. I do not mean only that events follow in a necessary order, but that they unfold according to justice and fair measure, in line with the true worth of each thing. Keep watching for this, as you have begun to do. And whatever you do, make sure it is something a truly good person would do. Hold to this principle in every action.

text:
Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth,
 or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see
 what it is in very truth.
plain_text: Do not think the way the person who wrongs you thinks, or the way they want you to think. Look at the matter itself and see what it truly is.

text:
These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do
 nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme
 part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee.
plain_text: Keep these two rules always ready. First, do nothing except what reason — acting from the highest part of you — suggests for the good of others.

text:
And
 secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to
 turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to
 change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any
 pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable
 apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be
 furthered; or from some other such inducement.
plain_text: Second, if someone can correct you or show you that you are mistaken, be always ready to change your mind. But let this change come not from wanting pleasure or praise, but always from a clear sense of justice, or from the common good, or from some other honest reason.

text:
Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if
 thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
plain_text: Do you have reason? Yes. Then why do you not use it? If your reason does its work, what more could you need?

text:
As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now
 shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot
 thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational
 substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated. Many
 small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops first
 and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
plain_text: Until now you have existed as a separate part. Soon you will dissolve back into the common substance of the one who brought you into being — or rather, you will be taken back into that original rational source from which all things have come. Many small pieces of incense sit on the same altar. One falls and burns first, another after. In the end it is all the same.

text:
Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of
 them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of
 reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.
plain_text: Within ten days, if things go well, those same people who now would see you as nothing better than an animal or a fool — if you return to your principles and to honoring reason — will think of you as a god.

text:
Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs
 over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
plain_text: Do not live as though you had a thousand years. Death is close. While you are still alive, while you still can — be good.

text:
Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know
 what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only
 what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in
 Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but
 to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant
 agitation.
plain_text: How much time and peace of mind a person gains by not caring about what their neighbor has said, or done, or tried to do — but only about what they themselves are doing, so that it may be right and good. As Agathos put it: do not look around at the faults of others, but run straight along your own path, without wandering or distraction.

text:
He who is greedy of credit
and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom
he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise
that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession
of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct. But
suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory with them
should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to thee after thou art
dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise?
plain_text: Whoever craves fame and reputation after death does not consider that the very people who remember them will also soon die, one after another — and those who come after them as well — until all memory, passed from one generation of admirers to the next, is finally gone. But suppose those who remember you, and your memory with them, were to last forever — what good would that do you? I will not ask what it matters once you are dead. But even while you are alive, what use is praise?

text:
But only for a secret and
politic consideration, which we call
οἰκονομίαν, or
dispensation. For as for that, that it is the gift of nature, whatsoever is
commended in thee, what might be objected from thence, let that now that we are
upon another consideration be omitted as unseasonable. That which is fair and
goodly, whatsoever it be, and in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and
goodly, it is so of itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a
part or member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either
better or worse.
plain_text: Unless it serves some practical purpose — what the Greeks call management or wise arrangement. But set that aside, since we are considering another matter. Whatever is truly beautiful and good — in whatever way it is beautiful and good — is so in itself, complete in itself. Praise is no part of it. What is praised is not made better or worse by the praise.

text:
This I understand even of those things, that are commonly
called fair and good, as those which are commended either for the matter
itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is truly good, what can
it stand in need of more than either justice or truth; or more than either
kindness and modesty? Which of all those, either becomes good or fair, because
commended; or dispraised suffers any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in
itself, or more vile if it be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple?
plain_text: I say this even about ordinary things that are called beautiful or good — things praised for their material or their craftsmanship. As for what is truly good, what more does it need beyond justice, truth, kindness, and modesty? Which of these becomes good because it is praised, or suffers harm because it is criticized? Does an emerald become worse or less valuable if no one praises it? Does gold, ivory, or purple?

text:
Is
there anything that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a
tree?
plain_text: Is there anything, no matter how common — a knife, a flower, a tree — that does?

text:
If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not
 believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How is
 the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies of them
 that are buried?
plain_text: If souls do survive after death (say those who doubt it), how can the air hold them all for eternity? And I ask in return: how has the earth been able all this time to hold the bodies of those who are buried?

text:
For as here the change and resolution of dead bodies into
 another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place for other dead
 bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the air, after they have
 conversed there a while, are either by way of transmutation, or
 transfusion, or conflagration, received again into that original rational
 substance, from which all others do proceed: and so give way to those
 souls, who before coupled and associated unto bodies, now begin to subsist
 single.
plain_text: For just as the breaking down and transformation of dead bodies into something else makes room for more bodies, so too the souls that pass into the air after death, having remained there for a while, are changed, absorbed, or taken back into that original rational substance from which all things come — and so they make room for the souls that, having been joined to bodies, now begin to exist on their own.

text:
This, upon a supposition that the souls after death do for a while
 subsist single, may be answered. And here, (besides the number of bodies,
 so buried and contained by the earth), we may further consider the number
 of several beasts, eaten by us men, and by other creatures. For
 notwithstanding that such a multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it
 were buried in the bodies of the eaters, yet is the same place and body
 able to contain them, by reason of their conversion, partly into blood,
 partly into air and fire. What in these things is the speculation of
 truth?
plain_text: This can be answered if we assume that souls survive for a time after death. And here, beyond the number of bodies buried in the earth, consider also the number of animals eaten by people and by other creatures. Even though such a great number are consumed every day and, so to speak, buried within the bodies of those who eat them, the same space can hold them all, because they are transformed — partly into blood, partly into air and fire. What is the search for truth in these matters?

text:
to divide things into that which is passive and material; and that
 which is active and formal.
plain_text: It is to divide things into what is passive and material, and what is active and gives form.

text:
Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire,
 to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the
 true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
plain_text: Do not lose your way. With every impulse and desire, do what is just. Always take care to see every impression that comes to you for what it truly is by nature.

text:
Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me;
 nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto
 thee is seasonable. Whatsoever thy seasons bear, shall ever by me be
 esteemed as happy fruit, and increase. O Nature! from thee are all things,
 in thee all things subsist, and to thee all tend. Could he say of Athens,
 Thou lovely city of Cecrops; and shalt not thou say of the world, Thou
 lovely city of God?
plain_text: Whatever is good for you, O World, is good for me. Nothing that comes at the right time for you can be too early or too late for me. Whatever your seasons bring, I will welcome as good fruit. O Nature, all things come from you, all things exist in you, and all things return to you. If the poet could say of Athens, "Dear city of Cecrops," can you not say of the world, "Dear city of God"?

text:
They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt
 live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man to
 confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as reason
 in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the goodness, but
 that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually proceed.
plain_text: People often say, "Do not take on too many things if you want to live happily." It is certainly best to limit yourself to necessary actions — only those that reason, in a being who knows it was born for community, requires. This brings not only the happiness that comes from doing good, but also the happiness that comes from doing fewer things.

text:
For
 since it is so, that most of those things, which we either speak or do,
 are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs follow that he
 shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble, and therefore at
 every action a man must privately by way of admonition suggest unto
 himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the number of
 unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off actions only,
 but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary for so will
 unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and cut off.
plain_text: Since most of what we say and do is unnecessary, cutting it away will give you more time and less trouble. At each action, ask yourself quietly: "Could this be one of those unnecessary things?" And you should cut away not only unnecessary actions, but unnecessary thoughts and daydreams too — for that is how you prevent the unnecessary actions that would follow from them.

text:
Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with
 those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of
 this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and
 fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in
 the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now trial of
 this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto
 perfect simplicity. Doth any man offend?
plain_text: Try living the life of a good person — someone who is content with whatever falls to their lot amid the changes and chances of the world, and who finds satisfaction in the rightness of their present actions and the goodness of their intentions going forward. You have tried the other kind of life. Now try this one. Stop troubling yourself any further. Bring yourself to complete simplicity. Does someone wrong you?

text:
It is against himself that he
 doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which of all the common chances
 of the world from the very beginning in the series of all other things
 that have, or shall happen, was destinated and appointed unto thee. To
 comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to
 gain the present time with best discretion and justice. Use recreation
 with sobriety.
plain_text: It is against himself that he does wrong — why should it bother you? Has something happened to you? It is fine. Whatever it is, it was part of the natural order of things from the very beginning, destined and assigned to you. To sum it all up in a few words: our life is short. Make the most of the present moment with good judgment and fairness. Enjoy rest and pleasure in moderation.

text:
Either this world is a κόσμος, or
 comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order: or if
 it be a mixture, though confused, yet still it is a comely piece. For is
 it possible that in thee there should be any beauty at all, and that in
 the whole world there should be nothing but disorder and confusion? and
 all things in it too, by natural different properties one from another
 differenced and distinguished; and yet all through diffused, and by
 natural sympathy, one to another united, as they are?
plain_text: Either this world is a well-ordered whole, arranged and governed by design, or it is a mixture — confused, perhaps, but still holding together. For how could there be any order within you, and nothing but chaos in the world itself? Especially when all things in it, though different from each other by nature, are also connected and united to one another through a natural bond.

text:
A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an
 hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish
 disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a
 fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world,
 that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well,
 that wonders at the things that are done in it?
plain_text: A dark and hostile character, a weak character, a hard and unforgiving character, a savage character, a timid character, a childish character — dull, dishonest, mocking, deceitful, tyrannical. What of it? If a person who does not know what exists in the world is a stranger to it, then the one who is surprised by what happens in it is just as much a stranger.

text:
He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are
 sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding. He
 poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all things
 needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being
 discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world, doth as
 it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's rational
 administration. For the same nature it is that brings this unto thee,
 whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world.
plain_text: The true runaway is the one who flees from reason, which connects us to each other. The truly blind person is the one who cannot see with the mind's eye. The truly poor person is the one who depends on others and does not have within himself everything he needs for life. The one who is a sore on the world is the one who, by resenting what happens to him, cuts himself off from the rational order of nature. For the same nature that brings you whatever happens also brought you into the world in the first place.

text:
He raises
 sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own soul
 from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.
plain_text: The one who stirs up rebellion in the city is the one who, through irrational actions, pulls his own soul away from the one shared soul of all rational beings.

text:
There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without
 so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked,
 neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith one.
 But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and yet I
 depart not from reason.
plain_text: One person practices philosophy without even a coat. Another does so without even a book. "I am half naked and have no bread to eat," says one, "and yet I do not abandon reason." And I say: I lack the nourishment of good teaching and guidance, and yet I do not abandon reason.

text:
What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to
 affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life
 as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs
 unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either
 tyrannically or servilely towards any.
plain_text: Whatever skill or trade you have learned, devote yourself to it and find contentment in it. Live the rest of your life as one who, with all your heart, entrusts yourself and everything you have to the gods. And toward other people, be neither domineering nor submissive.

text:
Consider in my mind, for example's sake, the times of Vespasian:
 thou shalt see but the same things: some marrying, some bringing up
 children, some sick, some dying, some fighting, some feasting, some
 merchandising, some tilling, some flattering, some boasting, some
 suspecting, some undermining, some wishing to die, some fretting and
 murmuring at their present estate, some wooing, some hoarding, some
 seeking after magistracies, and some after kingdoms. And is not that their
 age quite over, and ended? Again, consider now the times of Trajan.
plain_text: Picture in your mind the age of Vespasian. You will see the same things as now: people marrying, raising children, falling sick, dying, fighting, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, boasting, being suspicious, plotting, wishing for death, complaining about their situation, falling in love, hoarding money, chasing political office, and reaching for power. And is not that whole age now over and gone? Now picture the age of Trajan.

text:
There
 likewise thou seest the very self-same things, and that age also is now
 over and ended. In the like manner consider other periods, both of times
 and of whole nations, and see how many men, after they had with all their
 might and main intended and prosecuted some one worldly thing or other did
 soon after drop away, and were resolved into the elements.
plain_text: There too you see the very same things, and that age is also over and gone. Think the same way about other times and whole nations. See how many people, after pouring all their energy into chasing some worldly goal, soon after dropped away and returned to the elements.

text:
But especially
 thou must call to mind them, whom thou thyself in thy lifetime hast known
 much distracted about vain things, and in the meantime neglecting to do
 that, and closely and unseparably (as fully satisfied with it) to adhere
 unto it, which their own proper constitution did require. And here thou
 must remember, that thy carriage in every business must be according to
 the worth and due proportion of it, for so shalt thou not easily be tired
 out and vexed, if thou shalt not dwell upon small matters longer than is
 fitting.
plain_text: But especially remember those people you have known in your own lifetime who spent their energy on empty things, while neglecting to do what their own nature truly called for — and to hold to it wholeheartedly. Here you must also remember that the effort you give to each task should match its true importance. That way you will not wear yourself out or become frustrated by spending too long on small matters.

text:
Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become
 obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and
 famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names. Camillus,
 Cæso, Volesius, Leonnatus; not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus,
 then Adrianus, then Antoninus Pius: all these in a short time will be out
 of date, and, as things of another world as it were, become fabulous. And
 this I say of them, who once shined as the wonders of their ages, for as
 for the rest, no sooner are they expired, than with them all their fame
 and memory.
plain_text: Words that were once common are now strange and outdated. In the same way, the names of people who were once well known and famous are now nearly forgotten. Camillus, Caeso, Volesius, Leonnatus — and not long after, Scipio, Cato, then Augustus, then Hadrian, then Antoninus Pius. All of these will soon seem like figures from another world, almost like legends. And this is true of those who were the wonders of their time. As for everyone else, they are forgotten the moment they die.

text:
And what is it then that shall always be remembered? all is
 vanity. What is it that we must bestow our care and diligence upon? even
 upon this only: that our minds and wills be just; that our actions be
 charitable; that our speech be never deceitful, or that our understanding
 be not subject to error; that our inclination be always set to embrace
 whatsoever shall happen unto us, as necessary, as usual, as ordinary, as
 flowing from such a beginning, and such a fountain, from which both thou
 thyself and all things are.
plain_text: What, then, will always be remembered? Nothing — all is vanity. What should we give our care and effort to? Only this: that our minds and intentions be just, that our actions be kind, that our words be honest, that our understanding not be deceived, and that we be always willing to accept whatever happens to us as necessary, as ordinary, as natural — as flowing from the same source from which you yourself and all things come.

text:
Willingly therefore, and wholly surrender up
 thyself unto that fatal concatenation, yielding up thyself unto the fates,
 to be disposed of at their pleasure.
plain_text: Willingly and completely surrender yourself to that chain of causes. Yield yourself to fate, to be carried wherever it leads.

text:
Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence;
 all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves,
 incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change and
 alteration. Use thyself therefore often to meditate upon this, that the
 nature of the universe delights in nothing more, than in altering those
 things that are, and in making others like unto them. So that we may say,
 that whatsoever is, is but as it were the seed of that which shall be.
plain_text: Whatever exists now, whatever comes into being from day to day — all objects of memory, and the minds and memories themselves — consider that all things exist through change and transformation. Train yourself to reflect on this often: the nature of the universe takes delight in nothing more than in changing what exists and making new things like them. So we may say that everything that is, is like a seed of what will be.

text:
For
 if thou think that that only is seed, which either the earth or the womb
 receiveth, thou art very simple.
plain_text: If you think that only what is planted in the earth or conceived in a womb counts as a seed, you are thinking too narrowly.

text:
Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to
 that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and
 perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external
 accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou
 shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is, to
 be just in all his actions.
plain_text: You are now close to death, and yet you have not reached that perfect simplicity. You are still troubled and unsettled, still not free from fear of what may happen from the outside. You are not yet as gentle toward everyone as you should be, and not yet fully devoted to the one true study and wisdom — being just in everything you do.

text:
Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and
 those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are
 afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
plain_text: Look closely at the state of other people's rational minds. Even those the world considers wise — notice what they fear and run from, and what they chase after.

text:
In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist,
 nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy
 body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul. Wherein
 then, but in that part of thee, wherein the conceit, and apprehension of
 any misery can subsist? Let not that part therefore admit any such
 conceit, and then all is well.
plain_text: Your harm does not exist in another person's mind. Nor does it exist in any condition of your body, which is just a shell or a dwelling for your soul. Where does it exist, then? Only in that part of you where the idea and feeling of misery can take hold. Do not let that part accept such an idea, and all will be well.

text:
Though thy body which is so near it should
 either be cut or burnt, or suffer any corruption or putrefaction, yet let
 that part to which it belongs to judge of these, be still at rest; that
 is, let her judge this, that whatsoever it is, that equally may happen to
 a wicked man, and to a good man, is neither good nor evil. For that which
 happens equally to him that lives according to nature, and to him that
 doth not, is neither according to nature, nor against it; and by
 consequent, neither good nor bad.
plain_text: Even if your body — which is so close to it — is cut, burned, or left to decay, let the part that judges these things remain at peace. Let it judge this way: whatever can happen equally to a bad person and to a good person is neither good nor evil. For what happens alike to those who live according to nature and to those who do not, is neither in line with nature nor against it — and therefore neither good nor bad.

text:
Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living
 substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are
 terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion as
 it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that are,
 concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of
 connection and concatenation all things happen.
plain_text: Always think of the world as one living being, with one soul. Consider how everything in the world feeds into one shared awareness, and how everything is moved by one common impulse, as if by the will of that single soul. Consider how all things work together to cause one another's existence, and how all events are linked and connected.

text:
What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as
 Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and
 down?
plain_text: What are you, setting aside the better and divine part, but — as Epictetus rightly said — a poor soul carrying around a corpse?

text:
To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to
 attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and
 swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the
 world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away, another
 succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
plain_text: To undergo change cannot be harmful, just as coming into being through change is no special benefit. The time of the world is like a rushing river made up of everything that happens. As soon as one thing appears and passes, another takes its place, and that too will soon vanish from sight.

text:
Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature,
 as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer. Of the
 same nature is sickness and death; slander, and lying in wait, and
 whatsoever else ordinarily doth unto fools use to be occasion either of
 joy or sorrow. That, whatsoever it is, that comes after, doth always very
 naturally, and as it were familiarly, follow upon that which was before.
plain_text: Whatever happens in the world is, in the course of nature, as normal as a rose in spring and fruit in summer. Sickness and death are of the same kind, as are slander and scheming, and all the other things that usually cause fools either joy or sorrow. Whatever comes next always follows naturally and closely upon what came before.

text:
For thou must consider the things of the world, not as a loose independent
 number, consisting merely of necessary events; but as a discreet
 connection of things orderly and harmoniously disposed. There is then to
 be seen in the things of the world, not a bare succession, but an
 admirable correspondence and affinity.
plain_text: For you should see the events of the world not as a random collection of things that merely had to happen, but as a connected whole, arranged in order and harmony. What you find in the world is not just one thing after another, but a remarkable pattern of connection and relationship.

text:
Let that of Heraclitus
never be out of thy mind, that the death of earth, is water, and the death of
water, is air; and the death of air, is fire; and so on the contrary.
plain_text: Never forget what Heraclitus said: the death of earth is water, the death of water is air, the death of air is fire — and so in reverse.

text:
Remember
him also who was ignorant whither the way did lead, and how that reason being
the thing by which all things in the world are administered, and which men are
continually and most inwardly conversant with: yet is the thing, which
ordinarily they are most in opposition with, and how those things which daily
happen among them, cease not daily to be strange unto them, and that we should
not either speak, or do anything as men in their sleep, by opinion and bare
imagination: for then we think we speak and do, and that we must not be as
children, who follow their father's example;
plain_text: Remember also the one who did not know where the road was leading. And consider how reason — the very thing that governs all things in the world, the thing people are most closely connected to — is the very thing they most often resist. The things that happen every day never stop seeming strange to them. We should not speak or act as if in our sleep, guided only by habit and imagination — for even in dreams we think we are speaking and acting. And we should not be like children who simply copy their parents,

text:
for best reason alleging their
bare καθότι
παρειλήφαμεν; or, as by successive tradition from our forefathers we have received it.
plain_text: whose best reason for anything is simply, "This is how it has always been done" — handed down from one generation to the next.

text:
Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt
 certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert
 extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to
 die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the
 difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die
 rather many years after, than the very next day.
plain_text: If one of the gods told you that you would certainly die tomorrow, or the day after, you would not — unless you were extremely cowardly — think it a great advantage to die the day after rather than tomorrow. For what is the difference? In the same way, do not think it matters much whether you die many years from now or the very next day.

text:
Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who
 once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their
 patients, are dead and gone themselves.
plain_text: Think often about how many doctors, who once frowned so seriously and so dramatically over their patients, are now dead and gone themselves.

text:
How many astrologers, after that
 in great ostentation they had foretold the death of some others, how many
 philosophers after so many elaborate tracts and volumes concerning either
 mortality or immortality; how many brave captains and commanders, after
 the death and slaughter of so many; how many kings and tyrants, after they
 had with such horror and insolency abused their power upon men's lives, as
 though themselves had been immortal; how many, that I may so speak, whole
 cities both men and towns: Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and others
 innumerable are dead and gone.
plain_text: How many astrologers, after making a great show of predicting other people's deaths. How many philosophers, after writing so many long works on death and immortality. How many great generals and commanders, after the killing and slaughter of so many. How many kings and tyrants, after using their power over people's lives with such cruelty, as if they themselves would never die. And how many entire cities — Helice, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and countless others — are now dead and gone.

text:
Run them over also, whom thou thyself, one
 after another, hast known in thy time to drop away. Such and such a one
 took care of such and such a one's burial, and soon after was buried
 himself. So one, so another: and all things in a short time. For herein
 lieth all indeed, ever to look upon all worldly things, as things for
 their continuance, that are but for a day: and for their worth, most vile,
 and contemptible, as for example, What is man? That which but the other
 day when he was conceived was vile snivel; and within few days shall be
 either an embalmed carcass, or mere ashes.
plain_text: Go through the list of people you yourself have known who, one after another, have passed away. One person took care of another's funeral, and was soon buried himself. Then another, and another — and all of it in a short time. This is the main point: always look at worldly things as lasting only a day, and as being, in their real worth, small and passing. Consider what a human being is: just the other day, at conception, a tiny bit of matter — and in a few days, either an embalmed body or a handful of ashes.

text:
Thus must thou according to
 truth and nature, throughly consider how man's life is but for a very
 moment of time, and so depart meek and contented: even as if a ripe olive
 falling should praise the ground that bare her, and give thanks to the
 tree that begat her.
plain_text: In truth and according to nature, you must deeply consider that a person's life is only a brief moment, and so depart from it gently and content — like a ripe olive that falls and is grateful to the ground that held it and the tree that grew it.

text:
Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though
 the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are
 those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
plain_text: You must be like a cliff by the sea. The waves beat against it without end, yet it stands firm, and the churning waves around it are calmed.

text:
Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I,
 to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither
 wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come. For as for this, it might have happened unto any man, but any man having
 such a thing befallen him, could not have continued without grief. Why
 then should that rather be an unhappiness, than this a happiness? But
 however, canst thou, O man!
plain_text: "How unlucky I am, that this has happened to me!" No — say instead: "How lucky I am, that even though this has happened, I carry on without grief, neither hurt by the present nor afraid of the future." This could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on without being crushed by it. So why call the event bad luck rather than calling your response good fortune? But tell me, can you really

text:
term that unhappiness, which is no mischance
 to the nature of man I Canst thou think that a mischance to the nature of
 man, which is not contrary to the end and will of his nature? What then
 hast thou learned is the will of man's nature? Doth that then which hath
 happened unto thee, hinder thee from being just? or magnanimous? or
 temperate? or wise? or circumspect? or true? or modest? or free? or from
 anything else of all those things in the present enjoying and possession
 whereof the nature of man, (as then enjoying all that is proper unto her,)
 is fully satisfied?
plain_text: call something unhappy when it does no harm to human nature? Can you call something a misfortune for human nature when it does not go against the purpose and will of that nature? What have you learned that the will of human nature is? Does what has happened to you stop you from being just? Or brave? Or self-controlled? Or wise? Or careful? Or honest? Or modest? Or free? Or from having any of those qualities that, when present, fully satisfy human nature?

text:
Now to conclude; upon all occasion of sorrow remember
 henceforth to make use of this dogma, that whatsoever it is that hath
 happened unto thee, is in very deed no such thing of itself, as a
 misfortune; but that to bear it generously, is certainly great happiness.
plain_text: To conclude: whenever sorrow comes, remember this principle from now on — that whatever has happened to you is not, in itself, a misfortune. But to bear it with grace is truly a great happiness.

text:
It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual
 remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the
 examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long
 time enjoy their lives. What have they got more, than they whose deaths
 have been untimely? Are not they themselves dead at the last? as
 Cadiciant's, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus, or any other who in their lifetime
 having buried many, were at the last buried themselves.
plain_text: It may be a simple and rough remedy, but it works well against the fear of death: think about those who clung greedily to life for as long as they could. What did they gain over those who died young? In the end, are they not dead all the same? Cadicianus, Fabius, Julianus Lepidus — or anyone else who in their lifetime buried many others, only to be buried themselves at last.

text:
The whole space of
 any man's life, is but little; and as little as it is, with what troubles,
 with what manner of dispositions, and in the society of how wretched a
 body must it be passed! Let it be therefore unto thee altogether as a
 matter of indifferency. For if thou shalt look backward; behold, what an
 infinite chaos of time doth present itself unto thee; and as infinite a
 chaos, if thou shalt look forward. In that which is so infinite, what
 difference can there be between that which liveth but three days, and that
 which liveth three ages?
plain_text: The whole span of any person's life is small. And small as it is, consider what troubles, what moods, and what a frail body it must be lived with. Let it all be a matter of indifference to you. For if you look backward, there is an endless stretch of time behind you. And if you look forward, an equally endless stretch ahead. In something so vast, what difference is there between a life of three days and a life of three generations?

text:
Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most
 compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both
 words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For
 such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling,
 and ostentation.
plain_text: Always take the shortest path. The shortest path is the one that follows nature — that is, in everything you say and do, to follow what is most honest and right. This resolve will free you from all trouble, conflict, pretending, and showing off.
